newsitem.title: GERMANY: German officials demand pension scheme overhauls.
newsitem.headline: German officials demand pension scheme overhauls.

text.p: Germany's pension system must be overhauled as it can no longer cope with changing demographics and the nation's persistently high unemployment rate, officals warned at the weekend.

Dieter Hundt, president of Germany's federal employer association BDA told German newspaper Berliner Morgenpost: "A new formula for pensions is unavoidable. Pensions need to take into account the changing demographics and Germany's high jobless rate."

At the same time Guido Westerwelle, party secretary for Chancellor Helmut Kohl's junior coalition partner Free Democrats, said the FDP would make pension reform one of the party's key objectives next year.
As Germans are living longer but retiring earlier, Westerwelle said job-training schemes and the time spent studying at university must be shortened.
"The topic of pension reforms can no longer be taboo," he told German newspaper Express. He also said state pension schemes must be augmented by private savings.

BDA's Hundt said that Germany's average pension rates of 72 percent of an employee's salary could not be maintained over the long term. Firms already face an increase in costs of 7.4 billion marks through next year's increase in pension contributions to 20.3 percent, Hundt said.
Hundt also urged that private contributions for health insurance be increased and that competition among insurers be stepped up.
